design_detail: Cross-sectional comparison in early abstinence followed by a one-month retest with a retested control group. 27 non-treatment-seeking adults with current DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence lived on a UCLA research ward with urine-verified abstinence and were tested after 4–9 days (mean 6.19); 28 healthy comparison participants recruited the same way were tested as outpatients. 18 users (after a mean 25.44 days) and 21 controls (after a mean 43.50 days) were retested. Battery of 18 test scores in five domains, analysed by domain MANOVA, a composite standardized to the controls, and change scores.
can_establish: How this screened, advertisement-recruited group in its first week of verified abstinence compared with controls on a mostly verbal battery, and whether their test scores changed over the next three to four weeks more than controls' scores changed on retest.
cannot_establish: Whether the baseline differences were caused by methamphetamine (no pre-use data; groups differed in education and smoking), whether cognition changes after longer abstinence, or that no meaningful change occurs in the first month (the change estimate is too imprecise to exclude a moderate or large one).

sample.recruitment: Newspaper and Internet advertisements for both groups; users were not seeking treatment and resided at the UCLA General Clinical Research Center for the study (Method › Participants, 1st paragraph; Procedure). Payment: $30 per assessment, $50 for completing both, and $60 per week of residence for users.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Users: current DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence (SCID) and a positive urine test for methamphetamine at enrolment. Excluded for everyone: neurological disease (including head trauma with loss of consciousness over 5 minutes), systemic, cardiovascular or pulmonary disease, symptomatic hepatitis or cirrhosis, HIV infection, prescription psychotropic medication, and frank structural abnormality on MRI. Users excluded if they currently met abuse or dependence criteria for any drug other than methamphetamine except cannabis abuse, or had a current mood or psychotic disorder unrelated to methamphetamine. Controls: no methamphetamine use, no substance abuse or dependence, no illicit drug other than cannabis used more than twice (Method › Participants, paragraphs 1 and 4).
sample.demographics: Users vs controls at time 1 (Table 1): age 33.9 (7.5) vs 33.3 (7.9); men 17/27 vs 14/28; education 12.7 (1.9) vs 15.1 (2.5) years (p<0.01); mother's education 13.3 (2.6) vs 14.2 (2.2); Shipley-Hartford vocabulary 28.1 (4.6) vs 29.4 (4.3); Wender Utah Rating Scale 24.7 (17.2) vs 17.3 (18.2); cigarette smokers 21 vs 13 (p<0.01); White 17 vs 19. Hepatitis B positive 4 vs 2. Two users had substance-induced mood disorder, one substance-induced psychotic disorder, one social phobia; one control had a specific phobia (Method › Participants, 3rd and 4th paragraphs).
sample.attrition: 9 of 27 users (33%) chose not to stay 30 days and 7 of 28 controls (25%) did not return (Method › Participants, 5th paragraph). Users who left did not differ from completers on demographics, smoking, education, Wender Utah score, use history, vocabulary, or time-1 domain and composite scores (all p>0.05, statistics not shown). Control completers were older (35.19 vs 27.57 years, p<0.05), had marginally higher vocabulary (30.25 vs 26.20, p=0.06) and differed on the attention/processing-speed domain at time 1 (Results › Change between first and second assessments, 1st paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Advertisement-recruited, non-treatment-seeking users who agreed to live on a research ward, screened free of HIV, other substance dependence, psychiatric and medical comorbidity; the authors note this limits generalization to the wider population of people with methamphetamine dependence (Discussion, last paragraph). Retest data come only from users willing to stay a month. Control completers differed from control dropouts in age and vocabulary.

exposure.measurement: SCID DSM-IV diagnosis of current methamphetamine dependence; urine positive for methamphetamine at enrolment; frequency, quantity, duration and route by self-report (Method › Participants, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported: use on 4.15 (2.24) days per week; 5.87 (3.46) times per day on use days; about 4.66 (5.76) g per week; regular use for 7.63 (6.89) years. Usual route: smoking 68%, snorting 12%, injection 16%, oral 4% (Method › Participants, 2nd paragraph; Table 1).
exposure.polysubstance: Dependence on other drugs excluded; 3 users met cannabis abuse criteria; both users with and without that diagnosis averaged fewer than 2 days of cannabis use in the past 30 days. Six controls reported infrequent past cannabis use. Cigarette smoking 21/27 users vs 13/28 controls; nicotine dependence not assessed; participants could take smoking breaks during testing (Method › Participants, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Discussion, last paragraph). Alcohol use is not described for either group.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Users: on the research ward, urine drug screens every other day; first battery after at least 4 days of abstinence (mean 6.19, SD 1.47, range 4–9 days); retest after a mean 25.44 days (SD 3.20), i.e. about 31 days of verified abstinence. Controls: urine drug screen before each assessment (Procedure).

comparison.controls: 28 healthy volunteers recruited by advertisement, naive to methamphetamine, without substance abuse or dependence; tested as outpatients and retested after a mean 43.50 days (SD 15.81), longer than users because of scheduling delays (Method › Participants, 4th paragraph; Results › Change, 2nd paragraph).
comparison.matching: Not individually matched. No significant difference in age, sex, ethnicity, hepatitis B, Wender Utah score, mother's education or vocabulary; users had fewer years of education and more smokers (Results › First assessment, 1st paragraph). Education was used as a covariate in secondary analyses.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use testing. Premorbid ability estimated by Shipley-Hartford vocabulary (n.s., editors' d≈0.29 favouring controls) and mother's education (n.s., d≈0.37); own education differed by about 1.1 SD (editors' calculation from Table 1). Childhood ADHD symptoms by retrospective Wender Utah scale only (n.s., d≈0.42 toward more symptoms in users). The authors note that education may be either a premorbid marker or a consequence of use (Discussion, 5th paragraph).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: No substance abuse or dependence; no illicit drug other than cannabis used more than twice; 6 with infrequent past cannabis use; 13/28 smoked cigarettes; alcohol not described.

outcomes.instruments: Attention/processing speed: Trail Making A, Stroop words and colours. Working memory: backward digit span, Sentence Span, Missing Digit Span. Learning/memory: Selective Reminding Test (12 trials; total and intrusions), Repeated Memory Test (word and picture recall and recognition). Timed executive: Trail Making B, Stroop colour-word, letter fluency (FAS). Untimed executive: computerized Wisconsin Card Sorting (perseverative errors), Discrimination Learning, Logical Problems. Premorbid estimate: Shipley-Hartford vocabulary (Measures). Several tests are the group's own adaptations without published norms.
outcomes.validity_norms: Normative data were available only for Trail Making, Stroop, FAS, Selective Reminding and WCST; on these the users' time-1 means fell between the 16th and 55th percentiles (Discussion, 7th paragraph); which test sat at the 16th percentile, and the controls' percentiles, are not reported. Alternate forms were used at retest for all tests except Trail Making, Stroop and backward digit span (Measures, last paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: No individual impairment classification. Group differences by domain MANOVA, then t-tests only within domains with a significant omnibus test; a composite equal to the mean of test scores standardized to the controls' mean and SD; change = time 2 minus time 1 per test, analysed by domain MANOVA and as a composite change score standardized to the controls (Statistical methods). The authors define the impaired range as the 2nd percentile or below (Discussion, 7th paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Domain-wise MANOVA gatekeeping before individual t-tests (Statistical methods). Correlations of change with test interval and with use variables, and the paired practice-effect tests, were uncorrected (Results › Change, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; Discussion, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; testers could not have been blind to inpatient status.

analysis.effect_sizes: Time 1: composite −0.31 (0.45) in users vs 0.01 (0.60) in controls, t(53)=2.21, p<0.05 (Table 2; Results › First assessment, 3rd paragraph). The −0.31 is in units of the controls' test-level SDs; on the composite's own scale the standardized difference is about 0.60 (95% CI 0.06 to 1.14; editors' calculation from Table 2). Stroop colours 68.8 (10.5) vs 75.6 (11.7), t(53)=2.26 (editors' d≈0.61). Both became non-significant with education as a covariate (no adjusted estimates given). Learning/memory MANOVA p=0.09 and timed executive p=0.09, so individual tests were not tested; editors' approximate d from Table 2 (assuming about 26 per group): Selective Reminding total 0.67, Repeated Memory word recall 0.61, picture recall 0.90, word recognition 0.56, Stroop colour-word 0.65; near zero for Trail Making A and B, Stroop words, Sentence Span, Missing Digit Span and FAS. Change: no domain MANOVA significant (p>0.10); composite change 0.14 in users vs 0.00 in controls (standardized to controls' change), t(37)=−1.01, p=0.33; editors' d≈0.32 (95% CI −0.31 to 0.96). Time 2 (completers, Table 3; not tested by the authors): users remained below controls on Repeated Memory word recall (2.11 vs 4.14), picture recall (5.17 vs 7.29), word recognition (10.72 vs 14.67) and picture recognition (17.61 vs 20.24); editors' d≈0.73–0.82.
analysis.covariates: Education (time-1 Stroop colours and composite; change MANOVAs); test interval and vocabulary (change MANOVAs). Smoking, sex and Wender Utah scores not adjusted.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration mentioned. The time-1 hypotheses (deficits in verbal memory, executive functioning and attention/processing speed) were stated in advance in the Introduction; the authors state they had no specific hypotheses about change (Introduction, last paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Time-2 between-group comparisons are not reported although Table 3 shows sizeable differences on memory tests. MANOVA gatekeeping meant that medium-to-large memory differences at time 1 were not tested individually. Adjusted estimates after the education covariate are not given. Statistics for dropout comparisons and use-variable correlations are reported only as p>0.05.
analysis.power: Not reported; the authors attribute their null results partly to limited power (Discussion, 6th paragraph). Editors' approximation: about 44% power for a standardized difference of 0.5 at time 1 (27 vs 28) and about 33% for a change difference of 0.5 (18 vs 21), two-sided α=0.05.

interpretation_gap.results_show: After about 6 days of verified abstinence, users scored below controls on the composite (editors' d≈0.6, wide interval) and significantly on one processing-speed test; the differences were no longer significant when years of education was a covariate. Memory tests showed medium-to-large differences that were not tested because their domain MANOVA was p=0.09. Over about 25 days, users' change did not differ significantly from controls' change (editors' d≈0.32, 95% CI −0.31 to 0.96), and users still scored below controls on memory tests at retest (untested). On the five normed tests, users' means were between the 16th and 55th percentiles.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that users "do not show considerable cognitive gains in the first month of abstinence" and that a longer abstinence may be needed (Abstract, Conclusions). This is a no-change inference from a test with about one-third power whose interval includes a large differential improvement; the Discussion itself calls the indications of improvement equivocal (Discussion, 2nd paragraph). The abstract reports the 0.31-SD composite difference as significant but does not say it became non-significant after adjusting for education, a point the Discussion treats at length, raising the possibility that premorbid differences account for most of the variance (Discussion, 5th paragraph). The abstract's 0.31 SD is in test-level units and understates the standardized composite difference (about 0.6).

timeline.event: Longitudinal studies reporting improvement with abstinence (Chou et al., 2007; Jaffe et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2004) did not retest a control group, so practice effects cannot be separated (as summarized by Simon et al., Introduction, 5th paragraph).
Chang et al. (2005): users abstinent about a week did not differ from matched controls on a broad battery (as summarized by Simon et al., Introduction, 2nd paragraph).

Meta-analysis cited by Simon et al. for the largest user–control differences in learning (d=−0.66), executive functions (−0.63), memory (−0.59) and processing speed (−0.52) (Introduction, 1st paragraph; values as reported by Simon et al.).

Iudicello et al. (2010): over about 13 months, self-reported abstainers' global change was close to that of retested controls; larger gains confined to 6 abstainers impaired at baseline (appraised in sc_iudicello_2010 from this reading batch).

replication.where_it_stands: Both controlled retest studies in this batch find users' overall change close to that of retested controls, one over the first month with verified abstinence (this study) and one over about a year with self-reported abstinence (Iudicello et al., 2010); neither is precise enough to exclude moderate recovery, and both show that practice effects in controls are of the same order as the users' gains.

funding.funder: National Institutes of Health grants DA 022539, DA 020726 and DA 15179 and contract DA 50038, all awarded to Edythe D. London (title footnote).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement on the PMC page.
funding.affiliations_note: UCLA Department of Psychiatry and Biobehavioral Sciences and Semel Institute; two authors at the University of Southern California Department of Psychology. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A larger study (several dozen per group) of people with methamphetamine use disorder with biologically verified abstinence, retested at fixed intervals from the first week to a year alongside controls retested at identical intervals with alternate forms, with between-group comparisons reported at every time point, premorbid ability measured independently of education (for example school records), and pre-registered analyses.

domains.note: Groups differed by about 1.1 SD in education and in smoking (78% vs 46%); smoking and sex not adjusted; adjusting for education removed the time-1 differences, but education may partly be a consequence of use.
Current dependence by SCID, urine-positive at enrolment, abstinence verified every other day; use amounts self-reported.
Advertisement-recruited, non-treatment-seeking, heavily screened users willing to live on a ward; control retest completers older and with higher vocabulary than control dropouts.
Users were inpatients without treatment, controls outpatients; retest interval 25 vs 44 days.
33% of users and 25% of controls not retested (dropouts compared, statistics not shown); WCST data for only 13 controls and 18 users; FAS not analysable at retest.
Alternate forms for most tests, but several in-house tests without norms; no assessor blinding possible for inpatient status.
Pre-specified MANOVA gatekeeping, but time-2 group comparisons and education-adjusted estimates not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Abstinence is well verified and the retested control group is a real strength, but the time-1 user–control difference is confounded by education and smoking, and the change comparison is small, uses different settings and intervals for the two groups, and cannot separate a null from a moderate effect.

key_findings.finding: After a mean 6.19 days (range 4–9) of urine-verified abstinence, 27 users scored below 28 controls on the battery composite: −0.31 (0.45) vs 0.01 (0.60), t(53)=2.21, p<0.05.
key_findings.note: The 0.31 is in test-level SD units; the standardized difference on the composite is about 0.60, 95% CI 0.06 to 1.14 (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Only the attention/processing-speed MANOVA was significant at time 1; within it, users were slower on Stroop colours (68.8 vs 75.6, t(53)=2.26, p<0.05). Learning/memory and timed executive MANOVAs were p=0.09.
key_findings.note: The paper prints the MANOVA statistic as Wilks' lambda = 2.97, which is impossible for a lambda (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: The Stroop colours difference and the composite difference both became non-significant when years of education was entered as a covariate (no adjusted estimates given).

Memory tests not followed up because of the MANOVA gate showed medium-to-large differences at time 1: Selective Reminding total 110.3 vs 120.3; Repeated Memory picture recall 5.89 vs 8.11, word recall 2.56 vs 4.18, word recognition 11.30 vs 14.00 (editors' d≈0.56–0.90).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation assuming about 26 per group; exact per-test n is given only as 24–28 controls and 25–27 users.

key_findings.finding: Users' time-1 means on the normed tests (Trail Making, FAS, Selective Reminding, Stroop, WCST) fell between the 16th and 55th percentiles, which the authors describe as low-average to average and not in the impaired range (2nd percentile or below).
Neither days of abstinence before testing (4–9) nor years of use or grams per week were related to time-1 scores (all p>0.05, statistics not shown).
18 users (retested after 25.44 days, SD 3.20) and 21 controls (after 43.50 days, SD 15.81, p<0.01 for the difference) completed both assessments; 9 users and 7 controls were lost.
key_findings.locator: Method › Participants, 5th paragraph; Results › Change between first and second assessments, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: No domain MANOVA on change scores differed between groups (p>0.10), with or without education, interval or vocabulary as covariates. Composite change was 0.14 in users vs 0.00 in controls, t(37)=−1.01, p=0.33.
key_findings.note: Editors' d≈0.32, 95% CI −0.31 to 0.96: compatible with no differential change and with a large one.

key_findings.finding: Across all participants, 7 tests improved significantly on retest (Trail Making A, Stroop colours, words and colour-word, Logical Problems, Discrimination Learning, Sentence Span; uncorrected paired t-tests), including tests given in alternate forms.

At retest, users still scored below controls on Repeated Memory word recall (2.11 vs 4.14), picture recall (5.17 vs 7.29), word recognition (10.72 vs 14.67) and picture recognition (17.61 vs 20.24); the paper reports no between-group test at time 2.
key_findings.note: Editors' d≈0.73–0.82 (approximate p 0.01–0.03), computed from Table 3 with 21 vs 18.

key_findings.finding: Within users only, a longer retest interval went with more improvement on Repeated Memory picture recognition and Logical Problems and less on backward digit span (uncorrected p<0.05); interval was unrelated to change in controls and across all participants.

reporting_issues.issue: MANOVA results are printed as Wilks' lambda = 2.97 (time 1) and 'all Wilks' lambdas < 1.36' (change); Wilks' lambda lies between 0 and 1, so these are presumably F statistics, printed without degrees of freedom.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › First assessment, 2nd paragraph; Results › Change, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The omnibus tests cannot be checked; the bound of 1.36 is uninformative as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The chi-square for sex is printed as 0.34 and for smoking as 6.82; from the Table 1 counts (17/10 vs 14/14; 21/27 vs 13/28 smokers) the uncorrected values are 0.94 and 5.72 (editors' calculation), whereas the printed ethnicity (0.15) and hepatitis B (0.83) values reproduce exactly.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › First assessment, 1st paragraph; Table 1

reporting_issues.issue: The route percentages (smoking 68%, snorting 12%, injection 16%, oral 4%) are exact for 25 participants (17, 3, 4, 1) and cannot be obtained from 27.
reporting_issues.consequence: Route missing for 2 users, not disclosed.

reporting_issues.issue: Retest intervals are 43.50 days (controls) and 25.44 days (users) in the Results and Procedure but 45 and 29 days in the Discussion.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Change, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the Results values are the reliable ones.

reporting_issues.issue: The note to Table 3 says data came from 19–17 users, but only 18 users completed both assessments.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor typographical error in the per-test n.

reporting_issues.issue: The vocabulary comparison is reported as t(50), implying 52 participants with vocabulary scores, and WCST data exist for only 13 controls and 18 users; Table 1 does not show these missing values.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › First assessment, 1st paragraph; Table 2 note
reporting_issues.consequence: Premorbid estimate and the untimed executive domain rest on incomplete data.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports the composite difference as significant without saying it was non-significant after adjusting for education, and expresses it as 0.31 SD in test-level units.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Results › First assessment, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers of the abstract cannot tell that the difference depends on whether education is adjusted, or that it is about 0.6 SD on the composite's own scale.
